extracted.intended_audience: Trademark applicants, trademark counsel, and USPTO examining attorneys (practitioners handling ex parte appeals to the TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evidentiary rules and best practices for filing and litigating ex parte trademark appeals to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (notice of appeal, requests for reconsideration/remand, briefs, exhibits, timing, and related Board/examining attorney actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for reconsideration filed with notice of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant files a request for reconsideration of a final action (or second refusal/repeated requirement) together with a notice of appeal, the request should be made by separate submission and the notice should indicate contemporaneous filing; if filed via ESTTA, check the box indicating a request for reconsideration is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will acknowledge receipt, suspend proceedings (including the time to file the appeal brief), and remand the application to the examining attorney for consideration. Because papers may become separated, indicate the request in the notice of appeal (or check ESTTA box). Do not file the appeal brief within sixty days of the notice of appeal when reconsideration is pending (37 CFR § 2.142(b)(1); see TBMP § 1204). If the examining attorney acts first, the Board will institute the appeal after that action and reset the appeal-brief due date as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect when reconsideration does not withdraw all refusals/requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after reconsideration, all refusals/requirements are not withdrawn and a new final refusal or action maintaining finality issues, omit the six-month response clause, return the application to the Board, resume appeal proceedings, and allow applicant time to file its appeal brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examining attorney approves for publication/registration, the appeal is moot and the examining attorney should notify the applicant by phone or e-mail. The examining attorney must issue a written Office action before returning the application to the Board indicating what was withdrawn/maintained and any accepted amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark examining attorney's appeal brief timing and service
rubrics_metrics.description: After the applicant's main appeal brief is received by the Board and the Board forwards the application to the examining attorney, the examining attorney must file an appeal brief within 60 days (or within an extension for that purpose) and must send a copy to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examining attorney's brief is late-filed, the Board may exclude it absent adequate explanation. Failure to file a brief does not result in automatic approval; the Board will decide the appeal without the benefit of the brief. See 37 CFR § 2.142(b)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawing grounds in the examining attorney's brief
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examining attorney determines a ground or requirement is no longer tenable, the examining attorney should state in the appeal brief that the refusal/requirement has been withdrawn; if not mentioned, the Board may treat it as withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the examining attorney does not explicitly state withdrawal, the Board may treat an unmentioned refusal/requirement as withdrawn (see TBMP § 1203.02(g)). If the examining attorney intends to add a new ground or requirement, a request for remand is appropriate (see TBMP § 1209.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for remand by examining attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examining attorney decides registration should be refused on an additional ground, make a new requirement, or suspend the application, the examining attorney should submit a written request that the application be remanded to him/her for further examination instead of preparing an appeal brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remand requests are governed by 37 CFR § 2.142(f)(6) and TBMP § 1209.02. A remand request is generally granted when made to assert a new refusal/requirement; if denied, the Board will reset the examining attorney's time to file an appeal brief. If a new final action issues after remand, do not include a six-month response clause and resume appeal with an opportunity to file a supplemental brief directed to the new issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply brief rules and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may file a reply brief within 20 days from the issue date of the examining attorney's appeal brief (or within an extension for that purpose), but filing a reply brief is not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply brief must not include a proposed amendment, a request for remand, or a request for an oral hearing in its body; such requests must be filed as separately captioned papers (see TBMP §§ 1205.01, 1207.02, 1216). The Board will notify the examining attorney of a reply brief. There is no rule for an examining attorney's written response to the reply brief, although the examining attorney may respond orally at oral hearing if one is requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of time to file an appeal brief (good cause standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may grant an extension of time for filing an appeal brief upon written request showing good cause; the determination considers all relevant circumstances, including prior extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons that have been found to constitute good cause include appointment of a new attorney, illness, need to get instructions from a foreign applicant, and negotiating a consent agreement. The Board may grant a short limited period (e.g., ten days) if a request is insufficient, or may grant an extension but warn no further extensions will be granted absent extraordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and evidence submitted with briefs (timeliness and record completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidentiary record in the application should be complete prior to filing an appeal; it is not necessary to attach as exhibits material already of record, and exhibits not made of record during examination are untimely and generally will not be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: if the opposing party discusses untimely exhibits without objection, they may be deemed stipulated into the record and considered (see TBMP § 1207.03). Evidentiary references in briefs unsupported by timely submissions may not be considered. Numerous cases illustrate when submissions with briefs were or were not considered; submissions with reply briefs are especially likely to be untimely unless previously made of record or later accepted via remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases which may be cited in briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since January 23, 2007, the Board permits citation to any Board decision, though decisions designated not precedential are not binding on the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing cases in a brief, include a citation to The United States Patent Quarterly (USPQ) if the case has appeared there (see TBMP §§ 101.03, 801.03). Citation of non-precedential opinions is permitted but not encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of claims or requirements by omission in brief
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant does not assert a claim made during prosecution in its appeal brief, the claim may be deemed waived; similarly, if an applicant complies with a requirement and the examining attorney does not discuss it, or the examining attorney does not discuss a ground for refusal in his brief, the requirement or refusal may be deemed withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better practice is to request remand when seeking to comply with a requirement rather than simply offering an amendment in the brief (see TBMP § 1205). Case citations demonstrate waiver consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of filing a request for reconsideration (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a request for reconsideration between a final action and the appeal period does not stay the time for filing an appeal or petition; a request filed more than six months after a final action is treated as a request for remand; once briefing has begun, a request for reconsideration is treated as a request for remand and should not be combined with the applicant's appeal brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant files both a timely request for reconsideration and a timely appeal and the examining attorney has not yet considered the request, the Board will acknowledge, institute the appeal, suspend proceedings, and remand. Where both are timely filed but the Board has not acted within sixty days, the applicant should not file its appeal brief because the Board will likely institute and remand. If reconsideration raises a new issue, the examining attorney must afford an opportunity to respond before issuing a new final refusal. If an appeal is late-filed but reconsideration was timely, the Board will inform the applicant the late appeal cannot be entertained and will forward the application to the examining attorney for consideration of the reconsideration request (see TBMP §§ 1202.02, 1204).

rubrics_metrics.name: New issues raised by reconsideration or amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the request for reconsideration or an amendment raises a new issue, the examining attorney must give the applicant an opportunity to respond before issuing a new final refusal and returning the application to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of new issues include seeking registration under § 2(f), seeking registration on the Supplemental Register, or amending the identification of goods/services where identification was not the subject of the final Office action. See TBMP § 1201.02 and TMEP §§ 714–715 for examples. The first Office action considering and refusing an amendment that raises a new issue must be a nonfinal action including a six-month response clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional evidence filed with a timely request for reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional evidence filed with a timely request for reconsideration (i.e., submitted before expiration of the six-month response period) will be regarded as part of the record on appeal, even if submitted after filing the notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examining attorney denies a reconsideration filed with a notice of appeal, a subsequent request for reconsideration is treated as a remand even if within six months, and additional evidence filed with the second request will become part of the record only if the request for remand is granted for good cause. See TBMP §§ 1207.02, 1209.04 and cases cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining attorney submitting new evidence during reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examining attorney, upon consideration of a request for reconsideration (with or without new evidence), is not persuaded and issues a new action, the examining attorney may submit new evidence directed to the issues for which reconsideration is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the action is nonfinal, the applicant may not submit additional evidence in response; the applicant must file a request for remand to submit additional evidence (see 37 CFR § 2.142(d) and cases cited). The Board's rules and case law govern when such evidence will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of application during appeal (procedure and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant files an amendment within six months of a final action or second refusal and also files an appeal, and the examining attorney has not yet acted on the amendment, the applicant should indicate in the notice of appeal (or check the ESTTA box) that an amendment/reconsideration has been filed; the Board will acknowledge, suspend proceedings, and remand to the examining attorney for consideration of the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's remand letter will instruct the examining attorney on acceptable further actions. The examining attorney may submit evidence related to the amendment but may not assert a new refusal/requirement or submit unrelated evidence unless a remand request under 37 CFR § 2.142(f)(6) is filed and granted. If the examining attorney accepts the amendment but maintains final refusal for other reasons, the Office action should indicate the amendment is accepted and remaining refusals; omit the six-month clause, return the application to the Board, and resume appeal with time for the applicant to file its brief. If the amendment raises a new issue and is refused, the first Office action must be nonfinal and include the six-month response clause.
